This is the English loan 'cashew', said kaashu. I am not sure how common it is in Ramallah compared with كاجو (kaaju), which I believe is the more usual Levantine word.
The spelling without waw points to kaffiyye, with doubled f and y. Taa marbuta after ي is e. Palestinians also say 7aTTa for the scarf.
beet has ee, and ج is a moon letter so the article stays il-: il-jdiid. The vowel in jdiid drops after ج, as is normal in Palestinian.
The word for spices is بهارات with ه, not ح; the given spelling looks like a typo. The short first a drops in speech: bhaaraat.
Palestinian turns ay into ee (as in beet, leele), so gheeme. Taa marbuta after م is e.
Form II past, ghayyar, with doubled y. maw3id keeps aw, though some speakers say moo3id, which is why confidence is medium.
3am + present tense with the b- prefix. I take the verb to be form II shatti (rain in winter), but form I btishti is also possible, so I am unsure. Palestinians also say 3am btmaTTir.
Loanword said intarnit, with the glottal written after il- as the scheme requires. mish goes with the participle maashi, 'working/going'.
Form II past with doubled z: wazza3. Everyday verb in Palestinian.

Said booza in the city, as in Jerusalem's booza shops; the formal spelling is بوظة. Taa marbuta after ز is e under the scheme. The capital C in the English is just a typo. Palestinians also say jilaati.
Feminine of mu3allim, with doubled l. Taa marbuta after م is e. Some speakers say mi3allme.
Bookish word used in forecasts and writing, so ق keeps [q]. In conversation people say Tuluu3 ish-shams.
haad is Palestinian 'this', and ق in 'amiiS is a glottal stop. biiji 3alayy, literally 'comes on me', is the idiom for 'fits me'.
ishi is the typical Palestinian 'something'. fii means 'there is'. غ is gh and ط is emphatic T.
Standard everyday word, pronounced shaari3.
MSA-origin plural that is normal in everyday Palestinian speech, as in khuDaar w fawaakeh. The final vowel is e; some speakers say fawaaki.
Gypsum or plaster, and also a medical cast: jibs.
The English marks it as formal. It is the forecast-register word, said Ta's with a glottal stop. In everyday speech people say il-jaww.
Active participle yaabis, meaning dry, hard or dried out, as of bread or soil. It is used in everyday Palestinian speech.
Understood and used across the Levant, including by Palestinians; the first vowel is short. There is no clearly more Palestinian single word to give.
The dual صحتين becomes Sa7teen (ay turns to ee). Taa marbuta after ي is e: 3aafye. Said to someone eating or after a meal.
ض is D. The causative form II wajji3 takes the bi- prefix, with the suffix -ni meaning 'me'. I am not sure whether it is said with or without the doubled j, biwaj3ni.
MSA-origin verb that is common in conversation. Urban speech turns ذ into z in such borrowings, so i3tazar, not i3tadhar.
